versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then God said to Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel, and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”

2 So Jacob told his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your garments. 3 Then let us arise and go to Bethel. I will build an altar there to God, who answered me in my day of distress. He has been with me wherever I have gone.”
4 So they gave Jacob all their foreign gods and all their earrings, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.

5 As they set out, a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons. 6 So Jacob and everyone with him arrived in Luz (that is, Bethel) in the land of Canaan. 7 There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.
8 Now Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried under the oak below Bethel. So Jacob named it Allon-bacuth.

9 After Jacob had returned from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him. 10 And God said to him, “Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel.” So God named him Israel.

11 And God told him, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you. 12 The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you.”
13 Then God went up from the place where He had spoken with him.

14 So Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker—and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil. 15 Jacob called the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.

context_lines: After the violence at Shechem, God tells Jacob to go to Bethel and build an altar to the God who met him when he fled Esau. Jacob calls the household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change their clothes. He explains the journey by recalling the God who answered him in distress and has been with him wherever he went.

The household surrenders its idols and earrings, which Jacob buries near Shechem. As they travel, terror from God restrains the surrounding cities from pursuing them. At Bethel, Jacob builds the commanded altar. The account also records the death and burial of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, preserving the household's grief within the story of return.

God appears again, confirms Jacob's name as Israel, and renews the promises of descendants, nations, kings, and the land given to Abraham and Isaac. The God who has watched over Jacob now reaffirms the same family promise for the generations ahead.

Jacob sets up a stone pillar where God has spoken, pours a drink offering and oil on it, and again names the place Bethel. The return brings the earlier encounter and vow back into view. It also calls the whole household to a loyalty that must affect what they keep and how they live.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand the return as a renewal of worship and loyalty to God, accompanied by His confirmation of the promise. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 35:1–11](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) connect the outward removal of idols and preparation for worship with a needed change of heart.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: God's faithfulness calls for a changed life within the people He preserves. [Titus 2:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/titus/2.htm) joins saving grace with learning to reject ungodliness and becoming a people eager to do good. That wider theme helps explain why returning to Bethel involves putting away rival gods as well as remembering an earlier blessing.

The promise of kings also reaches forward within the Bible's larger story. [Luke 1:31–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/1.htm) announces Jesus as the Son who receives David's throne and reigns over the house of Jacob forever. Genesis does not yet name those later kings, but the promise to this troubled family belongs to the history that leads to Christ.
